newsitem.title: ANGOLA: IMF returns to Angola with emergency programme.
newsitem.headline: IMF returns to Angola with emergency programme.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday it believed the Angolan government was serious about economic reform and pledged to set up a three-year emergency programme worth up to $75 million.

"We are talking about an emergency programme of three years which will be funded with our own money and will mean an upfront imbursement," IMF managing director Michel Camdessus told a news conference.
The IMF withdrew its representative from the oil and mineral-rich country last year after the MPLA-led government failed to implement reforms for the fourth time since 1987.
But after three days of talks with President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and his recently reshuffled government, Camdessus said he was confident things had changed.
"I see a change in the economic orientations of the government compared with only one year ago," he said.

"I have seen the determination and courage with which this new government is taking difficult steps and has already succeeded in reducing significantly the hyper-inflation, which is still at an unacceptable level."
Angolan inflation is running at over 1,300 percent.
The new government had a "good chance" if it continued on its economic reform programme aimed at introducing a disciplined and transparent budget, he said.
The emergency programme under the Extended Structural Adjustment Facility will make available up to 25 percent of the Angola's $300 million quota.
It will be aimed at reconstructing the country's war-shattered economy and specifically help with the reintegration of about 100,000 demobilised Angolan government and rebel troops.

Camdessues said an IMF team would arrive in Angola within the next few days to begin negotiations with the government on the terms of the three-year programme, which should be approved by the IMF baord in December or January.
Speaking before departing from Luanda for Mozambique, he said he had decided to take the "risk" of investing in Angola after assurances from both the government and former rebel group UNITA.
"Today I have enough confidence in the peace process and in the government's determination to bring about economic stability for the transistion to a market economy," he said.
The IMF programme would pave the way for support from other institutions including the World Bank and Angola's creditors, he added.
But Camdessus stressed the participation of the IMF was conditional on the full implementation of the Lusaka protocol, a peace agreement signed by the Angolan government and UNITA in 1994.
"We want to see the full implementation of the Lusaka protocol...If full implementation is not achieved the IMF will reassess the situation," he said.
Camdessus said the time had come for the international community to contribute financially to Angola's development.
"I have decided to take the risk and tell the international community that the moment has arrived to add financial support...not just humanitarian aid," he said.
